definition_verbatim:
Approach 1 (of 2) - focuses on organization, equipment, selection and training to distinguish SOF from regular forces; SOF's main role is to complement general military effort in different sorts of operations; views role of SOF as limited military operations of a unique nature - a figurative sharpshooter carrying out narrowly focused precision military operations

Elite units that can carry out missions which either cannot be performed by regular units at all, or cannot be performed by them at an acceptable cost
explanation: Approach 1 - SOF can 'exceed the routine capabilities of conventional military forces'; SOF 'are personnel who receice specialized training to execute tasks behind enemy lines in support of conventional military operations or counterinsurgency campaign' (Terry White); SOF are 'most capable troops sent to take care of the most difficult missions' (James Dunnigan)
source_MLA: Leslau, Ohad. "Worth the Bother? Israeli Experience and the Utility of Special Operations Forces." Contemporary Security Policy 31.3 (2010): 509-30. Print.
sub_source:
Maurice Tugwell and David Charters, ‘Special Operations and the Threats to United States Interests in
the 1980s’, in Frank R. Barnett, B. Hugh Tovar, and Richard H. Shultz (eds), Special Operations in US
Strategy (Washington DC: National Defense University Press, 1984), p. 34.

definition_verbatim:
Approach 2 (of 2) - emphasizes uniqueness of SOF's operations and objectives; sees role of SOF as more expansive, a force that can be used to win the hearts and minds of the local population - a social worker role in addition to military support

Unmatched capabilities and ability to undertake missions that do not fall within conventional military tasks -- humanitarian assistance, insurgency, counterinsurgency missions, etc.
explanation: Approach 2 - SOF 'are not just ordinary military operations writ small; they are qualitatively different from those of most regular units' (Edward Luttwak et al); SOF 'conduct operations that are outside the realm and tactics of the conventional battlefield' (Susan Marquis); SOF operations are 'unexpected strokes of violence, usually mounted and executed outside the military establishment of the day, which exercise a startling effect on the enemy; preferably, at the highest level' (M.R.D. Foot)
source_MLA: Leslau, Ohad. "Worth the Bother? Israeli Experience and the Utility of Special Operations Forces." Contemporary Security Policy 31.3 (2010): 509-30. Print.

definition_verbatim:
Units that specialize in performing small scale, clandestine, covert or overt operations of an unorthodox and frequently high-risk nature, undertaken to achieve significant political or military objectives in support of foreign policy

The two approaches do not conflict, but rather complement one another, and Special Operations Forces could and should - under the right circumstances - fulfill both functions
source_MLA: Leslau, Ohad. "Worth the Bother? Israeli Experience and the Utility of Special Operations Forces." Contemporary Security Policy 31.3 (2010): 509-30. Print.

term_raw: Special Operations Forces (as defined by others)
definition_verbatim: Generally composed of unique forces specific to particular country requirements, therefore they exhibit few commonalities internationally other than a shared 'elite' status; tend to be the part of any defence force often glorified by the media and the entertainment industry, but that remain shielded behind the closed doors of government security policy and (more often) self-imposed secrecy
source_MLA: Brailey, Malcolm. "Not Many Jobs Take a Whole Army: Special Operations Forces and the Revolution in Military Affairs." Thesis. Institute of Defence and Strategic Studies Singapore, 2004. Print.

definition_verbatim: Those elements of legitimate state-based military forces that are specifically selected, trained and organised to carry out 'special operations' and which provide those same states with a unique capability of high strategic utility
source_MLA: Brailey, Malcolm. "Not Many Jobs Take a Whole Army: Special Operations Forces and the Revolution in Military Affairs." Thesis. Institute of Defence and Strategic Studies Singapore, 2004. Print.

definition_verbatim:
An inherently agile instrument ideally suited to the ambiguous and dynamic irregular environment while allowing national and collective defence establishments to retain freedom of action through employing economy of force. They operate outside the realm of conventional operations or beyond the standard capabilities of conventional forces, thus providing a solution to extraordinary circumstances of political interest when no other option is available

Years of training, education, and experience acquired through an investment in time and resources are necessary to prepare SOF units to successfully perform special operations
explanation: SOF are characterized as strategic assets because of their ability to achieve political, military, psychological, and informational objectives that represent the foundational instruments of national power
source_MLA: United States of America. National Security Agency. North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Special Operations Forces Study. By NATO Special Operations Coordination Centre. N.p.: n.p., 2008. Print.

definition_verbatim: Military activities conducted by specially designated, organized, trained and equipped forces using operational techniques and modes of employment not standard to conventional forces. These activities are conducted across the full range of military operations independently or in coordination with operations of conventional forces to achieve political, military, psychological and economic objectives. Politico-military considerations may require clandestine, covert or discreet techniques and the acceptance of a degree of physical and political risk not associated with conventional operations.
source_MLA: United States of America. National Security Agency. North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Special Operations Forces Study. By NATO Special Operations Coordination Centre. N.p.: n.p., 2008. Print.
sub_source: NATO Glossary of Terms and Definitions

definition_verbatim:

(Include US Army Special Forces units (Green Berets), US Army Rangers, special mission units, the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment, Civil Affairs (CA) and Psychological Operations forces (PSYOP), US Navy SEALs, US Air Force Special Tactics teams, and fixed wing and rotary wing air assets)
discipline:

definition_verbatim: "Small-scale, clandestine, covert or overt operations of an unorthodox and frequently high-risk nature, undertaken to achieve political or military objectives in support of foreign policy. Special Operations are characterized by either simplicity or complexity, by subtlety and imagination, by the discriminate use of violence, and by oversight at the highest levels. Military and nonmilitary resources, including intelligence assets, may be used in concert."
source_MLA: Byars, William R. Combined Control of Special Operations Forces in the Central Region of Allied Command Europe. Rep. Alabama: Air War College Air University, 1989. Print.

definition_verbatim:
"No mission was too difficult or dangerous when our country was called."

"No group of aviators has come close to matching the Special Operators' skills and versatility."

"These operations had an immense real and psychological impact on our adversaries; vastly exceeding the nominal investment on our part."
source_MLA: Chinnery, Philip D. Any Time, Any Place: Fifty Years of the USAF Air Commando and Special Operations Forces, 1944-1994. Annapolis, MD: Naval Institute, 1994. Print.

definition_verbatim: Small, carefully selected military, paramilitary, and civilian units with unusual (occasionally unique) skills, which are superlatively trained for specific rather than general purposes, and are designed to undertake unorthodox tasks that ordinary units could accomplish only with far greater difficulty and far less effectiveness, if at all.  SOF, however, are not needed for all special operations.
source_MLA: Collins, John M. Green Berets, Seals, and Spetsnaz: U.S. and Soviet Special Military Operations. Washington: Pergamon-Brassey's, 1987. Print.

definition_verbatim: Like a carpenter's combination tool, SOF provides a wide variety of capabilities for the CINC's operational toolbox. In war, SOF exploits enemy weaknesses, as a combat multiplier for conventional forces, and sets conditions for operational success. In operations short of war, where conventional forces are constrained by political limitations, SOF provides a means to achieve the strategic ends for the theater. In short, as the political influence on the operational continuum increases, the application of SOF increases as the ability to use conventional forces decreases.
source_MLA: Bonham, Gordon C. "Special Operations Forces: The Combination Tool in the CINC's Operational Toolbox." Thesis. Thesis / Dissertation ETD, 1991. Print.

definition_verbatim: Forces specifically organized, trained and equipped to conduct or support special operations. They pos- sess unique capabilities designed to address those missions, regardless of where they are conducted in the operational continuum
source_MLA: Bonham, Gordon C. "Special Operations Forces: The Combination Tool in the CINC's Operational Toolbox." Thesis. Thesis / Dissertation ETD, 1991. Print.
sub_source: The Joint Chiefs of Staff Publication 3-05 (JOS Pub 3-05), Doctrine for Joint Special Operations

definition_verbatim: SOF is, by doctrine, a joint force made up of Army, Air Force, and Navy Special Operations Forces. Although single service special operations are possible in concept, they are infeasible in practice. The execution of a special operation, from insertion to extraction, requires a joint air, ground, and maritime team to achieve mission success.
source_MLA: Bonham, Gordon C. "Special Operations Forces: The Combination Tool in the CINC's Operational Toolbox." Thesis. Thesis / Dissertation ETD, 1991. Print.

definition_verbatim: Special Operations Forces are an essential part of the . . . 'Total Army'. They perform critical functions complementing heavy and light forces in the middle and upper reaches of the conflict spectrum. They are generally the force of first choice for dealing with threats at the lower end of the conflict spectrum due to their regional expertise, language qualifications, austere support requirements, and lower visibility.
explanation: As evidenced by the Army's accomplishments of the past ten years, one must conclude Special Forces is alive and well, totally established in the Service and Joint communities, and viable, given the in-place systems. One must further conclude, however, that the dynamism of the global situation, an impending defense budget cut and a concomitant build-down of the Army pose potential problems for the future of Special Forces
source_MLA: Hilton, Corson L. "United States Army Special Forces: From a Decade of Development to a Sustained Future." Thesis. US Army War College, 1991. Print.
sub_source: (U)Special Operations Forces Modernization Action Program(SOFNAP)(S), HQDA, DCSOPS, August 1989, sec. 1,p.6.42

definition_verbatim: US special operations figure prominently in the new adaptive joint force packages that are being put together by US Atlantic Command (USACOM) in Norfolk, VA, to support the needs of US regional commanders-in-chief overseas. The new force packages, in particular, are designed to augment traditional peacetime rotational deployments of US Navy and Marine forces on ships overseas, which cannot by sustained at previous levels due to force structure cuts.
source_MLA: Goodman, Glenn W., Jr. Rangers Get Sealegs: Special Operations Play in New Joint Force Packages. Armed Forces Journal International 131:52 May '94. Print.

definition_verbatim: Employable where high-profile conventional forcess appear to be politically, militarily, and/or economically inappropriate; small, self-reliant, readily deployable units that capitalize on speed, surprise, audacity, and deception to accomplish missions in ways that minimize risks of escalation and concurrently maximize returns compared with orthodox applications of military power, which normally emphasizes mass
source_MLA: United States of America. Library of Congress. Congressional Research Service. Special Operations Forces: An Assessment 1986-1993. By John M. Collins. Washington, D.C.: Congressional Research Service, 1993. Print.

definition_verbatim:
First is the concept of being "global scouts." Special operations in the future will have forward presence with minimum forward bases -- forward present because of all our training missions. Those small groups can collect a lot of knowledge about their areas ... and relay information that can give regional CINCs and National Command Authorities a real feel for what is going on in that area. 

Second, we will be the pathfinders for the stratefy of engagement in the [next] century. Until we come up against a peer competitor in the future or a group of peer competitors, we think the idea of engagement and enlargement -- engagement with other nations to enlarge democracy and competitive markets -- will be an important part of what we do. Our soldiers will be doing that because of their cultural understanding, and we see in the future that will be more of our niche, even more than today. We also have a highly specialized direct-action capability, and those forces will remain force multipliers. Should we go from engagement and enlargement [to] conflict, when we make that very easy transition into doing direct action. For early forced entry, our forces will be the choice. We will be key "enablers" for our coalitions, providing for early integration into plans and operations and building mutual trust.

Our role will also be to serve as providers for peacekeeping and stability transitions. We can't do it all. The special operations forice is relatively small, so we are still going to need large forces for peacekeeping and stability -- brigades of soldiers to do that -- but the soldiers who will enable it to happen and be the ones who make the transition easy for the standard conventional commander will be psychological operations [PSYOP], civil affairs and Special Forces soldiers.
source_MLA: Steele, Dennis. Defining Army Special Ops' Role for the Next Century. Army 47:16-20 Apr '97. Print.

definition_verbatim:
SOF have determined that their soldiers will be more successful if they have the following attributes:
Organizational skills, trainability, situational awareness, ability to make complex discriminations and decisions, personal adaptability, resistance to stress, dependability, determination, and stability, and physical endurance and specialized military skills

SOF must select soldiers who can remain "mentally alive" while experiencing deep fatigue and personal discomfort.
source_MLA: Carlin, Thomas M. (Col) and Sanders, Mike. Soldier of the Future: Assessment and Selection of Force XXI. Special Warfare 9:16-21 May '96. Print.

definition_verbatim:
Unlike conventional forces, (SOF) usually work in small teams. They opreate behind enemy lines, train indigenous forces, or work with other countries to rebuild nations after war. Special operations forces may be most useful during periods of relative peace or "behind enemy lines" in major conflicts. This unconventional, often indirect, warfare has long been unappreciated or even disdained by conventional forces.

Special operations forces have developed unique operational capabilities and missions that distinguish them from their conventional counterparts. Each group performs missions and meets requirements that more conventionally trained or organized forces can not adequately address. The success of these operations has often required unconventional men and, occasionally, women.

They are nearly always commanded by conventional force commanders who are not trained in SOF capabilities and occasionally mistrust the forces.
source_MLA: Marquis, Susan L. Unconventional Warfare: Rebuilding U.S. Special Operations Forces. Washington, D.C.: Brookings Institution, 1997. Print.

definition_verbatim: Commando operations in the sense of self-contained acts of war mounted by self-sufficient forces operating within enemy territory are as old as warfare itself.
author: Thomas, David
source_MLA: Thomas, David. "The Importance of Commando Operations in Modern Warfare 1939-82." Journal of Contemporary History 18.4 (1983): 689-717.

term_raw: US Army Special Forces / UW [Thomas q. US doctrine]
definition_verbatim: In 1952, the US Army Special Forces were established for the purpose of waging what the army defined as 'unconventional warfare' in the rear... this form of warfare encompassed guerrilla warfare, escape and evasion, psychological warfare, and subversion. Thus, it had essentially nothing to do with commando operations in the proper sense.
author: Thomas, David (q. US Army doctrine)
source_MLA: Thomas, David. Journal of Contemporary History 18.4 (1983): 689-717.

term_raw: LRPG not a commando unit [Thomas, boundary]
definition_verbatim: the Long Range Penetration Group (LRPG), a large, independent raiding force, which operated on a self-contained basis behind Japanese lines... nor can this force be regarded as a commando unit in the strict sense.
author: Thomas, David
source_MLA: Thomas, David. Journal of Contemporary History 18.4 (1983): 689-717.

term_raw: special operations [Deruelle, by mission not operators]
definition_verbatim: The difference between these special operations and 'regular warfare' (battles, sieges) lay neither in numbers nor in the specialisation of soldiers, but in missions characterised by limited aims, surprise, tricks, stratagems, initiative taken at low levels of command, and constant adaptation.
author: Deruelle, Benjamin
source_MLA: Deruelle, Benjamin. "The sixteenth-century antecedents of special operations 'small war'." Small Wars & Insurgencies 25.4 (2014): 754-766.

definition_verbatim: a 'party' is 'a unit of soldiers that one sends to plunder, or to reconnoitre and ravage the enemy country'.
author: Richelet, Pierre (q. in Deruelle)
source_MLA: Quoted in Deruelle 2014 from Pierre Richelet, Dictionnaire Francois (1680).

definition_verbatim: a detachment is recognised a 'parti' if it has a 'written order from the commander, and if it counts at least... twenty foot soldiers or fifteen horsemen, or else they are considered brigands'.
author: Furetiere, Antoine (q. in Deruelle)
source_MLA: Quoted in Deruelle 2014 from Antoine de Furetiere, Dictionnaire Universel.

definition_verbatim: The execution of activities in a precise manner that employ SOF in hostile, denied or politically sensitive environments to seize, destroy, capture, exploit, recover or damage designated targets, or influence threats.
explanation: One pole of USASOC's special-operations continuum; contrast with special warfare.
author: USASOC (q. in Martin)
source_MLA: Quoted in Grant Martin, "Zero dark squared," International Journal 69.3 (2014): 418; from US Army JFK SWCS, "ARSOF 2022," Special Warfare (2013).

definition_verbatim: the execution of activities that involve a combination of lethal and non-lethal actions taken by specially trained and educated forces that have a deep understanding of cultures and foreign languages, proficiency in small-unit tactics, subversion, sabotage and the ability to build and fight alongside indigenous combat formations in a permissive, uncertain or hostile environment.
explanation: The other pole of USASOC's continuum; operator-heavy definition.
author: USASOC (q. in Martin)
source_MLA: Quoted in Grant Martin, "Zero dark squared," International Journal 69.3 (2014): 418; from US Army JFK SWCS, "ARSOF 2022," Special Warfare (2013).
